heading: Valley bridges, lodges and snow domes
intro: Structures built by and named by Indigenous peoples show the same ideas as this lab: frames, shells, cables in tension and loads carried to the ground. Here are a Cree name on an Edmonton bridge, the Niitsitapi (Blackfoot) lodge and the Inuit iglu and qaggiq. Each connection names a specific people and gives a source for every name.

connections.title: Tawatinâ Bridge: a valley crossing
connections.text: The Tawatinâ Bridge carries the Valley Line LRT across the North Saskatchewan River. The City of Edmonton says tawatinâ means "valley" in Cree. CBC reports that the City's Aboriginal relations officer and other advisors helped choose the name. Design firm DIALOG describes a 260 metre extradosed cable stayed bridge: 28 stay cables run from two pylons to a slender concrete deck. Under the train deck, a path for walking and biking has a ceiling of painted panels by Métis artist David Garneau. He chose not to write down their meaning, saying "Some Elder or storykeeper will have to bring that to life."

sources.title: Source of the name tawatinâ (valley, in Cree): City of Edmonton, Transforming Edmonton, Tawatinâ Bridge: Connecting people to downtown
CBC News: Plains Cree language used to name Edmonton LRT bridges (Aboriginal relations officer and advisors helped choose the name)
DIALOG: Major milestone reached for Edmonton's Valley Line LRT: tawatinâ Bridge connected (extradosed cable stayed, 260 m, 28 stay cables, two pylons)
CTV News Edmonton: Lasting legacy: Tawatinâ footbridge officially opens, features Indigenous artwork (crosses the North Saskatchewan River, 260 m, two levels)
CTV News Edmonton: Métis designer installing hundreds of art pieces above new Tawatinâ Bridge walkway (David Garneau quote)

connections.title: Niitoy-yiss: a frame of poles, a shell of hides
connections.text: Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, at Siksika, says the Siksika refer to themselves as Niitsitapi, "the Real People," and calls the Blackfoot tipi niitoy-yiss. The Canadian Encyclopedia explains that the Blackfoot Confederacy favoured a four pole foundation, while Cree and Dakota peoples typically used three poles. A sewn cover of bison skins was arranged over as many as 20 poles, and stones often held its edges to the ground. The Galt Museum and Archives says a lodge needed at least 16 hides to cover it fully. It adds that in lodges today, curtains are hung around the inside for extra warmth in winter.

sources.title: Source of the name Niitsitapi (the Real People): Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, Our Culture
Source of the name niitoy-yiss (Blackfoot tipi): Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, NIITOY-YISS: Blackfoot Tipi/Teepee
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Tipi (Blackfoot Confederacy four pole foundation; Cree and Dakota three pole; cover over as many as 20 poles; stones on edges)
Galt Museum and Archives: Blackfoot homes (Niitoiyiss; at least 16 hides; curtains in contemporary lodges)

connections.title: Iglu and qaggiq: domes of snow blocks
connections.text: The Canadian Encyclopedia says iglu means "house" in Inuktitut. Builders cut blocks of hard snow with knives of whale bone or metal and lay them in a spiral from the inside, so the walls lean inward into a dome. In Iqaluit, master builders Solomon Awa and Jacoposie Tiglik led a team that built a qaggiq, a large iglu used as a community gathering place. Maclean's reports it stood 20 feet high and 30 feet across, with its curve checked by experience, not instruments. Awa told CBC that "Inuit have traditionally been both artists and engineers." Nicole Luke, Inuk and Red River Métis, is an aspiring architect.

sources.title: Source of the word iglu (house, in Inuktitut) and of spiral, inward leaning snow block walls: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Igloo
Source of the name qaggiq (a larger iglu used as a community gathering place): Maclean's, How do you build an iglu that stands 20 feet tall? Very carefully
CBC News: Building anew on Inuit land (Solomon Awa quote; Nicole Luke, aspiring Inuk and Red River Métis architect)

try: Tawatinâ Bridge: which parts are in tension and which are in compression? Trace the load of a train from the deck, through the cables, to the pylons and down to the ground. Is the weight of the train a permanent or a non-permanent load? What about the weight of the concrete deck?

A Niitsitapi lodge combines categories. Which part is the frame and which part is the shell? The Canadian Encyclopedia says the cover could be held down with stones. Which non-permanent load would those stones help the lodge withstand? Compare a three pole and a four pole foundation: which shape do you think resists sideways pushes better, and how could you test it with craft sticks?

An iglu is a dome of snow blocks. Using Lesson 2, explain why it is a shell structure. Then use the snow load estimator from Lesson 4: if 10 cm of settled snow fell on a dome, is that a permanent or non-permanent load? Why might a large qaggiq need more care in its design than a small iglu?

slide.title: Valley bridges, lodges and snow domes
points: Edmonton: the Tawatinâ Bridge ("valley" in Cree) hangs its deck from cables in tension.
Alberta: the Niitsitapi niitoy-yiss is a frame of poles under a shell of hides.
Canada: Inuit build the iglu and qaggiq as domes of snow blocks laid in a spiral.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 1 (Beams, columns and arches) and Lesson 5 (Internal forces and deformation) for the Tawatinâ Bridge, and Lesson 2 (Mass, frame and shell) for the lodge and the iglu. The F1.K9 table on combining categories already lists a tipi; this slide names the specific Niitsitapi lodge and its source. Lab Bench, Investigation 3 (Structure spotter) is a good place to sort all three. Avoid describing painted lodge designs: Blackfoot Crossing says they are sacred. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing unsourced content (as asked): the lab's Coverage notes say "The tipi is described generally as a frame of poles with a cover (frame plus shell), and the Inuit snow house (iglu) as a dome-shaped shell of snow blocks. No specific community knowledge is described; please review this wording and consider a community partner." The deck's F1.K9 table lists "Tipi: None / Poles / Cover wrapped around" with the same review flag in its notes, and Lesson 2 mentions the iglu. Both are unsourced in the lab and deck. This draft builds on them with sources: the Niitsitapi niitoy-yiss (Blackfoot Crossing, Canadian Encyclopedia, Galt Museum) and the Inuit iglu and qaggiq (Canadian Encyclopedia, Maclean's, CBC). Would you like the lab wording changed to name the Niitsitapi lodge and cite these, or kept general?

The tipi row in the lab is generic. The Canadian Encyclopedia says pole foundations differ by nation (four poles for the Blackfoot Confederacy, three for Cree, Ojibwa and Dakota). Presenting one tipi as "the tipi" risks a pan-Indigenous generalization. Consider changing the table row to "Niitsitapi lodge (niitoy-yiss)" or "tipi (structures differ by nation)".

Names used and where each comes from: tawatinâ, "valley" (City of Edmonton; also CBC and CTV). DIALOG instead gives "big valley"; I followed the City. Niitsitapi, "the Real People," and niitoy-yiss (Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park). The Galt Museum spells it Niitoiyiss and Nitsitapi; I used Blackfoot Crossing's spelling. Should I confirm the preferred spelling with Siksika? iglu, "house" (Canadian Encyclopedia). qaggiq (Maclean's). CTV also gives amiskwacîwâskahikan as "beaver hills house"; I did not use it. I gave no translation for Siksika, Iqaluit or Kâhasinîskâk (the Connors Road bridge) because no fetched source gave one.

Tawatinâ Bridge: sources differ on the number of Garneau's panels (about 400 in CTV during installation, 500 on the City page, about 550 in CTV at the opening), so I gave no number. The Edmonton connection is a Cree name and a Métis artist's work; no source says Indigenous engineers designed the bridge. CBC says the City's Aboriginal relations officer and advisors helped choose the name, but does not name the Cree speakers or Elders involved. Is it worth asking the City who gifted or advised on the name? I described DIALOG as a design firm on the project; the page did not state its exact role.

Garneau deliberately did not write down the meaning of his artwork and said an Elder or storykeeper would need to bring it to life. I quoted that and did not interpret the panels. This could be a natural moment to invite an Elder or storykeeper on a class walk across the lower deck.

Alberta: Blackfoot Crossing writes about the tipi mostly in past tense and says painted tipi designs are sacred, given in dreams and transferred through a formal ritual. I left out all design and ceremony details and the place of honour. I used the Galt Museum line about curtains in lodges today to show this is a living practice. The Galt page is by Julius Delaney; it does not say whether he is Blackfoot. Would you like to invite a Siksika or other Niitsitapi Knowledge Keeper, for example through Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, to share how a lodge is set up? I did not find a well-sourced Stoney Nakoda lodge source in this session, so I did not use one.

Canada: CBC (2021, about 1,200 blocks, 65 square metres) and Maclean's (about 1,100 blocks, 20 feet high, 30 feet across) describe Solomon Awa's qaggiq builds; they may be different years, so I used only Maclean's size figures and gave no year. CBC says Awa was later mayor of Iqaluit; I left that out because I could not confirm it is current. Nicole Luke is described by CBC as an aspiring architect who contributed to designs in Cambridge Bay; please check her current status before naming her to students. Would you like to invite an Inuit Knowledge Keeper, for example through an Edmonton Inuit organization, to speak about iglu building?

I wrote that the snow blocks lean inward into a dome from the Canadian Encyclopedia. The claim that the dome works as a shell under compression is the lab's science framing, not a claim from an Inuit source. Please confirm that framing is acceptable. I did not fetch an Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami source this session, so the Canada connection does not use the term Inuit Nunangat in its text.

The iglu also appears in the Temperature and Heating Lab draft (g7-en2), about snow walls as insulation. This draft uses it only as a shell structure (blocks laid in a spiral, the qaggiq). Is it fine for both labs to use the iglu, or would you prefer a different Inuit structure here?
